source: NomadGrid editorial notes: general travel guidance, not part of the provided catalog.

Tokyo.tagline: Huge, safe and easy to get around once you have an IC card.
getting_around: A rechargeable IC card (Suica or Pasmo) works on almost every train, subway and bus: load it once and tap in and out.
Trains and the subway are the fastest way around. The last trains run around midnight, so plan your evening return.
Rush hour (about 7:30-9:30 am and 5-7 pm) is very crowded: avoid it with small children or luggage.
Taxis are safe but pricey; the rear door opens and closes by itself, so don't touch it.
etiquette: There is no tipping in Japan: leave the money, it can cause confusion.
Keep your voice low and phone calls off on trains.
Take your shoes off where you see a shoe rack or a raised floor.
Eating while walking is frowned on: stand by the stall or sit down.
Carry some cash: many small stalls and shrines do not take cards.
sightseeing_tips: Visit Senso-ji and Meiji Jingu early in the morning for calm and cooler air.
Many museums close one weekday: check the opening days shown for each sight in your plan.
Popular timed-entry attractions are best booked ahead.
good_to_know: Power sockets are type A at 100 V: bring an adapter.
Convenience stores are good for a cheap breakfast, snacks and cash machines that accept foreign cards.
Tap water is safe to drink.

Kyoto.tagline: Temples, gardens and old streets: best explored early and on foot.
getting_around: The subway has only two lines; buses reach most temples but get very crowded in the day.
Trains are quicker for Fushimi Inari (JR Nara line) and Arashiyama (JR Sagano line).
IC cards (Suica, ICOCA) work on Kyoto buses, trains and the subway.
The centre is flat and compact: cycling or walking is pleasant outside the hottest hours.
etiquette: In Gion, do not chase or block geiko and maiko for photos; some private lanes ban photography.
Be quiet in temples and shrines and never touch anything that is roped off.
Bow slightly at a shrine gate and walk to the side of the path, the centre is for the deity.
No tipping; carry some cash for small shops and temple entry.
sightseeing_tips: Arrive at Fushimi Inari or Kiyomizu-dera when they open to beat the crowds.
Most temples close in the late afternoon and stop admitting visitors earlier, so do them in the morning.
Leave an evening for a slow walk through Gion and the Kamo river bank.
good_to_know: Power sockets are type A at 100 V: bring an adapter.
Coin lockers at Kyoto Station are handy on check-out day.
Tap water is safe to drink.

Osaka.tagline: Japan's food capital: relaxed, loud and friendly.
getting_around: The subway and JR loop line cover most sights; an IC card (ICOCA, Suica) works on both.
Namba, Umeda and Shin-Osaka are the big hubs; allow extra time to change between them.
Taxis are fairly priced for short hops, useful late at night.
etiquette: On escalators, Osaka stands on the right (Tokyo stands on the left).
Do not eat while walking through crowded Dotonbori: stand by the stall.
No tipping; haggling is not done in shops.
Keep your voice low on trains.
sightseeing_tips: Dotonbori is best after dark, when the neon signs are lit.
Go to Universal Studios Japan at opening time and on a weekday if you can.
Osaka Castle grounds are free to walk; keep time for the museum inside only if you enjoy history.
good_to_know: Try takoyaki and okonomiyaki: they are the local specialities.
Power sockets are type A at 100 V: bring an adapter.
Tap water is safe to drink.

Dubai.tagline: Modern, spread out and air-conditioned: plan one area a day.
getting_around: The Dubai Metro and tram are cheap and air-conditioned: use a rechargeable Nol card.
Taxis are metered and easy to find; ride-hailing apps also work.
Distances are large: group sights by area (Downtown, Old Dubai, Marina) rather than crossing the city repeatedly.
Walking outdoors in the middle of the day is hot: use malls and metro links.
etiquette: Dress modestly in malls, souks and public places: covering shoulders and knees is a safe rule. Swimwear is for beaches and pools.
Public displays of affection and loud or rude behaviour are frowned on.
Ask before photographing people, and avoid photographing government buildings.
Alcohol is served only in licensed venues such as hotels.
Dress and behaviour expectations are stricter during the holy month of Ramadan; eating and drinking in public in daylight is discouraged then.
sightseeing_tips: Book the Burj Khalifa observation deck ahead, ideally for a sunset slot.
The Gold Souk and Al Fahidi are most pleasant in the cooler evening.
Global Village and outdoor parks open only for part of the year: check the opening days shown in your plan.
good_to_know: Power sockets are type G at 230 V: bring an adapter.
Carry a light layer: malls and the metro are strongly air-conditioned.
Tap water is safe but most visitors drink bottled water.

Abu Dhabi.tagline: Calmer than Dubai, with grand architecture and green spaces.
getting_around: Taxis are metered and ride-hailing apps work well: the city is spread out and not built for walking between sights.
Public buses need a rechargeable Hafilat card, but taxis are simpler for a short stay.
Plan one area a day: Corniche and the city, Saadiyat (museums), Yas Island (parks).
etiquette: At Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque cover arms and legs; women also cover their hair. Abayas can be borrowed at the entrance.
Visiting hours at the mosque change on Fridays: check before you go.
Speak softly inside the mosque and remove your shoes before entering the prayer halls.
Dress modestly in public places and ask before photographing people.
sightseeing_tips: Go to the Grand Mosque in the late afternoon for the best light and cooler air.
Louvre Abu Dhabi and the other Saadiyat museums have set closing days: check the days shown in your plan.
Corniche Beach is best in the morning or evening; the midday sun is strong.
good_to_know: Power sockets are type G at 230 V: bring an adapter.
Alcohol is served only in licensed venues such as hotels.
Carry a light layer for strong air-conditioning indoors.
